headline: A handful of healthy soil contains more organisms than people on Earth
universal_truth: The most important work often happens out of sight
fun_facts: One teaspoon of soil can contain 1 billion bacteria and miles of fungal threads
Earthworms turn over 10-15 tons of soil per acre per year—nature's plows
Dead leaves become soil through the work of billions of unseen decomposers
discussion_questions: What important work happens 'underground' in your life or organization?
Why do we rarely think about soil despite depending on it for all food?
What would happen if soil organisms stopped working?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: We walk on it without a thought. Dirt. Soil. The ground. But that brown stuff beneath your feet is the most alive place on Earth. A single handful contains more organisms than there are people on the planet. Soil isn't dead—it's teeming.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Every fallen leaf, every dead animal, every bit of organic matter—it all disappears into the soil. Where does it go? What invisible army breaks down everything that dies and recycles it into new life?
cliff.prompt: Who breaks down dead matter into soil?

options.text: Billions of bacteria, fungi, worms, and microorganisms working together
options.response: Yes. An invisible workforce of decomposers recycles all death into new life.

options.text: Chemical reactions break down organic matter over time
options.response: Chemistry is involved, but life does most of the work...

q1.title: Billions Per Teaspoon
q1.script: A single teaspoon of healthy soil contains up to 1 billion bacteria, yards of fungal threads, thousands of protozoa, and dozens of nematodes. You're standing on the most densely populated ecosystem on Earth.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Billions Per Teaspoon"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Earth's Recyclers
q2.script: Without decomposers, dead matter would pile up forever. Forests would be buried in their own leaves. Instead, bacteria, fungi, and invertebrates break everything down, releasing nutrients for new growth. Death feeds life feeds death—endlessly.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Worm Engineers
q3.script: Earthworms are soil engineers. They eat organic matter, digest it, and excrete nutrient-rich castings. They dig tunnels that aerate soil and help water penetrate. Darwin spent years studying worms—he knew they quietly transform the world.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: The most important work often happens out of sight. The billions of soil organisms ask no recognition yet make all visible life possible. Honor the unseen work—in nature and in life.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 66. Tomorrow, we'll discover the stories rocks tell. Until then, look at the ground differently—it's more alive than the world above it.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Underground Work - Honor the Invisible
growTrack.learning_objective: Recognize and appreciate unseen essential work
growTrack.activity: Identify someone whose essential work usually goes unnoticed—maybe someone who maintains systems, cleans up, or supports behind the scenes. Thank them today. Like soil organisms, they make visible life possible.
